name: Mnemic neglect
statement: People recall feedback that threatens a central part of their self-image worse than they recall the same feedback ascribed to somebody else.
meaning: The effect is a gap between two groups reading identical sentences. Participants take a bogus personality test and then read behaviours the test supposedly predicts. Half are told the behaviours describe them. Half are told they describe a stranger called Chris. The behaviours vary on two things: whether they are positive or negative, and whether the trait behind them is central to how a person sees themselves or peripheral. Recall drops in one cell only, negative behaviours on a central trait ascribed to the self. Sedikides, Green, Saunders, Skowronski and Zengel define the effect as inferior recall for self-threatening feedback compared with other kinds of feedback. Their model treats it as self-protection working at encoding: threatening feedback is processed shallowly and kept apart from stored self-knowledge, so a later memory search has few cues to find it by. That account predicts the effect should be specific to free recall, and it is. The same participants pick the same sentences out of a recognition test accurately, so the material is in memory.

origin.who: Constantine Sedikides and Jeffrey D. Green
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, volume 79, issue 6, pages 906-922
origin.note: The paper is titled 'On the self-protective nature of inconsistency-negativity management: Using the person memory paradigm to examine self-referent memory'. It reports three pilot studies and four experiments, and Experiment 1 tested 200 participants. The phrase 'mnemic neglect' is not in that title. The earliest title carrying it that a Crossref title search found on 21 September 2026 is Green, Pinter and Sedikides in 2005.

evidence: The founding experiment set the shape of everything after it. Sedikides and Green tested 200 participants, who answered 45 computer-administered items of a bogus instrument called the Michigan Omnibus Personality Inventory. Screens claimed it had been in use since 1984 and had gone to over 68,000 American college students in 1995 alone, then showed the scoring pass 25%, 50%, 75% and 100%. Participants read 32 feedback behaviours at their own pace, spent 2.5 minutes writing down as many of the United States as they could, and met a surprise recall task lasting 5 minutes. Two judges unaware of condition coded the recalled items to a gist criterion and agreed on over 98%. Intrusions ran at 5% of recalled behaviours and were removed, and two participants with three or more were dropped. In the self condition the proportion recalled was 0.39 for positive central behaviours and 0.31 for negative central ones. In the Chris condition the same sentences gave 0.36 and 0.40. Peripheral behaviours produced no such gap, 0.18 and 0.14 for the self against 0.17 and 0.15 for Chris. The three-way interaction that marks the effect was F(1, 192) = 6.39, p < .01. Averaged unweighted across the experiments reviewed by Sedikides and Green in 2009, in a table the 2016 review takes from Wells, the pattern repeats: self 0.42 positive central and 0.30 negative central, Chris 0.40 and 0.41. The recognition result is the load-bearing one for the model, and it comes from two experiments the paper keeps apart. Green, Sedikides and Gregg assigned 178 participants in Experiment 1 and entered 169 into the recall analysis, putting the 32 studied behaviours and 32 unstudied ones on the recognition test. Recall showed the usual gap. Recognition did not. Their intelligible accuracy index d sat at 0.86 and 0.88 for self central positive and negative, against 0.88 and 0.88 for Chris. The diagnostic three-way interaction came out at F(1, 146) < 1 on that index and on d prime. Accuracy was untouched, response bias was not: self participants were less ready than Chris participants to call central negative behaviours old, F(1, 160) = 5.48, p < .02. Experiment 2 added a bogus creativity test, assigned 232 participants and excluded 11. There the effect in recall emerged after ego-deflation and not after ego-inflation. It did not work by depressing recall of the threatening items, which did not differ between those conditions, t(108) = 0.65, p < .52. Recall of self-affirming behaviours was the part that moved, running higher after ego-deflation, t(108) = -3.49, p < .001. Recognition again showed nothing in either condition. Zengel, Wells and Skowronski ran four studies on when the effect appears. It survived a delay before recall and could not be put down to how long participants looked at each behaviour. It did not emerge under cognitive load, and their Studies 3 and 4 showed it waning when participants were occupied during encoding.

replication.headline: The effect holds, and it holds outside the group that named it. A meta-analysis of 93 samples by three authors with no tie to that group puts it at g = 0.365, and Leonard Newman's laboratory has run the paradigm four times without Sedikides or Green.
replication.detail: Liu, Deng and Yang pooled 18 studies and 93 independent samples, N = 4,989, and report g = 0.365, 95% CI 0.253 to 0.476, Z = 6.416, p < 0.001. Their abstract says most studies support the phenomenon while some find people attend to self-relevant negative information more rather than less. That figure also appears in this atlas under selective amnesia, entry 274, which is where the review's subtitle sends readers who look the phrase up. The concentration question is the one worth asking, because the programme ran for over a decade inside one collaboration. Newman's laboratory at Syracuse has run the paradigm four times with neither originator on the authorship, and the four do not all point the same way. In 2009, with Nibert and Winer, it reproduced the effect among participants low in defensive pessimism, total recall of negative central behaviours 1.67 for the self against 3.08 for Chris. Among those high in defensive pessimism it did not, 1.75 against 1.81. The review adds that the loss in the high group came largely from poor recall of the Chris behaviours. Those means are quoted here through that review, which is the only account of the paper obtained. In 2014, with Sapolsky, Tang and Bakina, it reported four experiments in which the length of the recall period and the way recalled behaviours are written down changed the results, which qualifies the paradigm rather than repeating it. In 2017, with Eccleston and Oikawa, two studies found more of the effect among Black students on a predominantly White campus than among other students, and priming egalitarianism reduced it. In 2025, with Tan, Zhang, Ni and Fang, one study found the effect in both American and Chinese participants and no sign it was larger in the American group. Other hands have run versions of it too. Liu and Yang tested Chinese middle-school students, and Matsumoto, Katahira and Kawaguchi published a revised paradigm with computational modelling in Cognitive Therapy and Research, where only the preprint is open and nothing is taken from it here. Mainz, Britz, Forster, Drüke and Gauggel recruited 75 healthy men at Aachen for anodal, cathodal or sham stimulation of the medial prefrontal cortex, with 25, 25 and 24 of them in the recall tables. All three groups showed the expected effect, which the stimulation did not shift. They used self-descriptiveness judgements of 80 trait adjectives rather than the Chris procedure, and the same study tested the self-serving bias, entry 109.

study.cite: Liu, W., Deng, L., & Yang, H. (2025). Embracing strengths and avoiding weaknesses: a meta-analysis of the mnemic neglect effect. Memory, 33(2), 278-294.

limits: The effect is easy to remove. It goes when memory is probed by recognition instead of recall, when participants are under cognitive load at encoding, and when self-threat is defused by self-affirmation, all reported in the 2016 review. Saunders ran three experiments and found it reversed in dysphoria, with dysphoric participants recalling self-threatening feedback better than non-dysphoric ones, and the review records two subsidiary analyses by Zengel and colleagues that did not reproduce that loss. Zengel, Skowronski, Valentiner and Sedikides report a loss of the effect among socially anxious individuals, and the review says their two experiments diverged. In their Experiment 1 the pattern held for both central trait dimensions, in Experiment 2 only for socially inept behaviours, and the review calls the inconsistency unresolved. Newman, Sapolsky, Tang and Bakina found the result sensitive to the recall procedure itself, which makes the length and format of the recall task a design choice with a result attached. On what was not obtained, every item retried on 21 September 2026. The Liu, Deng and Yang meta-analysis is closed access and was read in abstract only, at PubMed and at Semantic Scholar. Nothing is said here about which 18 studies it pooled, how it handled publication bias, or how heterogeneous the samples were. Taylor and Francis answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall page, so another reader may get through. That same challenge blocks Hogrefe for Newman, Sapolsky, Tang and Bakina, Guilford for Zengel, Skowronski, Valentiner and Sedikides, Springer for Liu and Yang, and Wiley for Newman, Nibert and Winer, whose article Unpaywall lists as a free published version. Brill is a plain paywall, offering the Tan article for purchase, and its landing page carries the abstract. The search covered Europe PMC by phrase, which returns 30 records, PubMed, which returns 15, Crossref by title, OSF registrations and preprints, and general web search, in English only. No preregistered direct replication of the Sedikides and Green procedure was found in any of those. OSF holds three registrations naming mnemic neglect, two on preferences for types of affection and one on moderators, and none of them re-runs that procedure.
misreadings: The commonest error is the one the review's own subtitle invites. 'Selective amnesia of one's faults' reads as a claim about life, and the measurement is a recall gap of a few behaviours, minutes after reading sentences generated by a fake personality test. Nothing here concerns autobiographical memory or forgetting real events. The second error is to read it as ordinary negativity bias. The comparison is against the identical sentences ascribed to Chris, and against peripheral traits, both of which recall fine. What the effect tracks is threat, not unpleasantness. The third is to treat the forgetting as loss. Recognition accuracy is intact, so the sentences are stored and the failure is at retrieval, which is why the model talks about encoding depth and cue linkage rather than erasure. Recognition is not wholly untouched, though: Green, Sedikides and Gregg found self participants more reluctant to call threatening items old, which they read as a further piece of self-protection. The fourth is to take g = 0.365 as a general property of self-relevant memory. It is an average across conditions that include ones where the effect vanishes and one clinical group where it turns around. A reader should also not assume the literature is one laboratory talking to itself. It began that way and has not stayed that way.

sources.text: Sedikides, C., Green, J. D., Saunders, J., Skowronski, J. J., & Zengel, B. (2016). Mnemic neglect: Selective amnesia of one's faults. European Review of Social Psychology, 27(1), 1-62. Accepted manuscript at the Strathclyde repository, downloaded twice to the same checksum and converted to text. The source for the definition, the paradigm, Table 1a and Table 1b, and the descriptions of Newman et al. 2009, Newman et al. 2014, Saunders 2011 and Zengel et al. 2015.

Sedikides, C., & Green, J. D. (2000). On the self-protective nature of inconsistency-negativity management: Using the person memory paradigm to examine self-referent memory. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 906-922. The founding paper. Obtained as the scanned reprint on Sedikides's Southampton faculty page, downloaded twice to the same checksum, with the pages read as images. The source for the 200 participants, the Michigan Omnibus Personality Inventory procedure and the Table 3 means. Closed at the publisher.

Liu, W., Deng, L., & Yang, H. (2025). Embracing strengths and avoiding weaknesses: a meta-analysis of the mnemic neglect effect. Memory, 33(2), 278-294. Closed access. Abstract read at PubMed via the E-utilities text endpoint and again at Semantic Scholar; the Taylor and Francis article page answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge. The source for g = 0.365 and its interval.

Newman, L. S., Nibert, J. A., & Winer, E. S. (2009). Mnemic neglect is not an artifact of expectancy: The moderating role of defensive pessimism. European Journal of Social Psychology, 39(3), 477-486. Unpaywall lists a free published version at Wiley, and Wiley answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge, so the paper is still unread here. Its means are quoted through the 2016 review.

Newman, L. S., Sapolsky, M. S., Tang, Y., & Bakina, D. A. (2014). What's recalled depends on the nature of the recall procedure: The case of mnemic neglect. Social Psychology, 45(2), 93-102. Abstract read in the Crossref record; Hogrefe answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge. The source for the four experiments and for recall period length and reporting format changing the results.

Newman, L. S., Eccleston, C. P., & Oikawa, M. (2017). Ignoring biased feedback: Membership in a stigmatized group as a moderator of mnemic neglect. The Journal of Social Psychology, 157(2), 152-164. Abstract read at PubMed; full text not obtained.

Tan, M., Newman, L. S., Zhang, B., Ni, J., & Fang, J. (2025). Mnemic Neglect in the United States and China: a Cross-cultural Investigation of Spontaneous Self-protection. Journal of Cognition and Culture, 26(1-2), 5-29, published online 14 October 2025 in a volume Brill dates 2026. Abstract read on the Brill landing page and again in the Crossref record; the full text is sold for 40 dollars and was not bought.

Zengel, B., Wells, B. M., & Skowronski, J. J. (2018). The waxing and waning of mnemic neglect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 114(5), 719-734. Abstract read at PubMed; the source for the four studies on delay, looking time and cognitive load.

Mainz, V., Britz, S., Forster, S. D., Drüke, B., & Gauggel, S. (2020). Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation of the Medial Prefrontal Cortex Has No Specific Effect on Self-referential Processes. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 14, 56. Full text read as the Europe PMC JATS XML; the source for the 75 men recruited, the group sizes in the recall tables and all three groups showing the effect.

Green, J. D., Sedikides, C., & Gregg, A. P. (2008). Forgotten but not gone: The recall and recognition of self-threatening memories. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 44(3), 547-561. Obtained as the published version on Sedikides's Southampton faculty page, downloaded twice to the same checksum and read as text. The source for both experiments, their samples, Table 1, Table 2 and the recognition bias result. The accepted version that Unpaywall points to, in the Southampton institutional repository, sits behind a proof-of-work bot challenge and could not be compared.

Saunders, J. (2011). Reversed mnemic neglect of self-threatening memories in dysphoria. Cognition and Emotion, 25(5), 854-867. Abstract read at PubMed; the source for the three experiments and the direction of the reversal. Full text closed and not obtained.

Zengel, B., Skowronski, J. J., Valentiner, D. P., & Sedikides, C. (2015). Loss of Mnemic Neglect Among Socially Anxious Individuals. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 34(4), 322-347. Closed access, and Guilford answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge. Described here through the 2016 review, which reports the divergence between its two experiments.

Liu, W., & Yang, H. (2023). The mnemic neglect effect in middle school students: a study based on two fundamental dimensions of social cognition. Current Psychology, 43(18), 16094-16103, published online 29 December 2023 and in print in 2024. Closed access, and Springer answers with a bot challenge. Cited as evidence that the paradigm is being run outside the originating group, not for its contents.

Matsumoto, N., Katahira, K., & Kawaguchi, J. (2022). Cognitive Reactivity Amplifies the Activation and Development of Negative Self-schema: A Revised Mnemic Neglect Paradigm and Computational Modelling. Cognitive Therapy and Research, 47(1), 38-51. Crossref record only; the published text is closed and the open copy is a preprint, whose figures are not used here. Cited for the existence of a revised paradigm run by another group.
